questions.q: A grocer in Nashik keeps spices in one corner and pulses and grains in another. His nephew rearranges the same shop so that all red packets sit together, all yellow ones together, and so on. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Both are classification, as each groups items by one common property
o: Both are classification, as each groups items by one common property
Only the grocer's is classification, as colour is not a property at all
Only the nephew's is classification, as it is based on appearance
Neither is classification, as only living things can be classified

questions.q:
Amma's kitchen in Kochi has 18 containers: 6 steel vessels and 3 clay pots that she cooks in, and 4 glass jars and 5 plastic boxes that store dry food. She keeps them on four shelves, one shelf for each material. Her son wants to use fewer shelves: one for cooking and one for storing. Then two new items arrive, a steel tumbler and a glass tumbler, used only for drinking water at the table.
(a) While cooking, Amma wants every container she may cook in on one shelf. Decide first: which arrangement suits her?
(b) Which property does each arrangement use, and how many groups does each make before the tumblers arrive?
(c) Where do the two tumblers go in each arrangement, and how many shelves does each arrangement then need?
(d) Her son says, 'Mine is better because it needs fewer shelves.' Using (b) and (c), say how much that saving shrinks once the tumblers arrive, and whether it is a strong reason.
questions.a: (a) The arrangement by use: all 9 cooking containers (6 steel, 3 clay) sit on one shelf, while by material they are split over the steel and clay shelves. (b) Amma's: the material, 4 groups (steel, clay, glass, plastic). Her son's: the use, 2 groups (cooking, storing). (c) By material, they join the steel shelf and the glass shelf, so it still needs 4 shelves. By use, they are neither cooked in nor used to store dry food, so a third group (drinking) is needed: 3 shelves. (d) The saving shrinks from 2 shelves (4 against 2) to 1 shelf (4 against 3), so 'fewer shelves' alone is a weak reason. The arrangement should be chosen by the property that serves her purpose, here the use.
s: Part (a): the arrangement by use chosen, since all 9 cooking containers sit together
Part (b): material, 4 groups; use, 2 groups
Part (c): steel and glass shelves (4 shelves); a new drinking group in the use arrangement (3 shelves)
Part (d): saving shrinks from 2 shelves to 1, so fewer shelves is a weak reason; purpose decides

questions.q:
Statement 1: Ten objects that have been grouped by shape cannot be grouped again by material, because a set of objects has only one correct classification.
Statement 2: The material chosen for an object depends on its properties and on the purpose for which the object is to be used.
Statement 3: Objects with similar functions can be made from different materials.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A games teacher wants a ball for a new game: when dropped from 1 m onto the cement floor, it must bounce back to between 30 cm and 50 cm. She tests three balls of about the same size from 1 m on the same floor: tennis ball 55 cm, cricket ball 25 cm, hand-exercise ball 10 cm.
(a) Does any of the three balls meet her rule? Check each one.
(b) Size, height and floor were the same for all three. What then explains the different bounces, and what should she look for in a new ball?
questions.a: (a) None: the tennis ball's 55 cm is above 50 cm, and the cricket ball's 25 cm and the hand-exercise ball's 10 cm are below 30 cm. (b) The balls are made of different materials, and different materials have different properties, so they bounce differently. She should look for a ball made of a material whose bounce lies between that of the tennis ball and the cricket ball.
s: Part (a): none fits, each bounce compared with 30 cm and 50 cm
Part (b): the material decides the bounce; a material that bounces between the tennis and cricket balls

questions.q: Tanvi puts a steel tumbler, a glass tumbler and a plastic tumbler in one group, and a steel spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon in another. Which common property has she used to group them?
questions.a: The shape and use of each object, since each group mixes several materials
o: The shape and use of each object, since each group mixes several materials
The material of each object, since steel and plastic appear in both groups
The hardness of each object, since every tumbler is harder than every spoon
The shine of each object, since only the metal objects were kept together

questions.q: Kabir grouped eight objects by colour and Nisha grouped the same eight by material. Kabir says: 'Both of us have classified correctly, and my colour groups are just as useful as Nisha's for choosing a material to make a water bottle.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Both have classified correctly, because each grouped the objects by one common property, and the same objects can be classified in more than one valid way. But for choosing a material for a water bottle, colour groups do not help; we choose a material by properties such as holding water, so Nisha's material groups are more useful.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: both are valid classifications by a common property
Wrong part: choosing a material depends on its properties and purpose, which colour groups do not show

questions.q: A shelf holds a steel spoon, a steel plate, a steel tumbler, a plastic spoon, a plastic tumbler, a glass tumbler, a glass plate and a wooden spoon. Sorted by material they form 4 groups. Sorted instead by kind of object (spoon, plate or tumbler), the group that mixes the most different materials contains ___ materials.

A school eco-club must place containers for (i) wet food waste from the canteen, (ii) broken glass from the laboratory and (iii) dry waste paper from classrooms. It has one each of: a cardboard box, a plastic bin with a lid, a metal bin and a cloth bag.
(a) Assign a container to each waste and give a property of its material that makes it suitable.
(b) For your assignment in (a), one container is left over. Which of the three wastes could it also hold safely, and why?
(c) Name the two containers that must never be used for broken glass, and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Any assignment with a correct property reason, e.g. food waste: plastic bin with a lid (plastic holds wet waste without soaking it up, and the lid keeps it covered); broken glass: metal bin (metal is hard, so sharp pieces do not cut through it); waste paper: cardboard box (the waste is dry and light, so a soft material is enough). A rigid plastic bin for glass or a metal bin for food waste is also accepted with a property reason. (b) Marked against the student's own leftover container: a cloth bag or cardboard box left over can hold the dry waste paper (dry and light); a metal bin left over can hold the broken glass or the food waste (hard, holds wet waste); a plastic bin left over can hold the food waste (holds wet waste without soaking it up). (c) The cloth bag and the cardboard box: both are soft materials that sharp pieces of glass would cut or tear through.
s: Food waste given a container with a correct property reason
Broken glass given a hard container with a property reason
Waste paper given a container with a reason
Part (b): a waste the student's leftover container can hold, with a property reason
Part (c): cloth bag and cardboard box, soft so glass cuts through

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cricket ball and a tennis ball of about the same size, dropped from the same height, bounce to different heights.
Reason (R): Balls for different sports are made of different materials, and different materials have different properties.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Sheeta's school bag has a body of cloth, a metal zip and plastic buckles on its straps. Ghulan's lunch box and his water bottle are both made of plastic.
(a) Why did the bag-maker use different materials for different parts of one bag? Use two of the parts in your answer.
(b) Which idea about materials does the bag show, and which idea do Ghulan's lunch box and bottle show?
questions.a: (a) Each part has a different job, so it needs a material with a different property: e.g. the zip must be hard so its teeth do not bend, while the body must fold and be light to carry. A material is chosen by its properties and the purpose of that part. (b) The bag shows that one object can be made of several materials; the lunch box and the bottle show that one material can be used to make more than one object.
s: Part (a): different parts have different purposes, so materials with different properties are chosen (two parts used)
Part (b): bag = one object, many materials; lunch box and bottle = one material, many objects

questions.q: A tumbler-maker folds four sample sheets into cups and pours 200 mL of water into each. After 5 minutes: cup W still holds 200 mL and keeps its shape; cup X holds 120 mL and its outside is wet; cup Y holds no water at all; cup Z holds 200 mL but has gone soft and bent over. Which sheet suits a tumbler for daily use?
questions.a: W, as it holds all the water and keeps its shape
o: W, as it holds all the water and keeps its shape
Z, as it also holds all 200 mL of the water
X, as it still holds more than half the water
Y, as water passing through lets it dry quickly

questions.q:
A student shows only her finished groups.
Group A: iron nail, copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon
Group B: wooden ruler, rubber eraser, paper sheet, jute bag
(a) Write the common property she must have used.
(b) Add one more object to each group.
(c) Suggest a different property that would split the objects of Group A into two groups.
questions.a: (a) Metal or not metal (equally, shiny or not shiny). (b) E.g. Group A: copper vessel; Group B: cardboard box. (c) E.g. by shape or use: long and thin (nail, wire) versus used in the kitchen (foil, spoon); any property that divides Group A.
s: Part (a): metal versus non-metal (or shiny versus not shiny) identified
Part (b): one correct extra object for each group
Part (c): a new property that actually splits Group A

questions.q: True or False? Steel, glass and plastic tumblers all do the same job, so the material chosen for a tumbler does not matter. Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Different materials can make objects with the same function only if each has the property the purpose needs; a tumbler's material must be able to hold water. Steel, glass and plastic can, but cloth or paper-like material cannot, so the material does matter.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the material must have the property the purpose needs (holding water); cloth or paper would fail

questions.q:
Each tray was meant to hold objects that share the property on its label, but one object in each tray does not belong. Match each tray (Column I) with the property that the misplaced object really has (Column II).
Column I
1. Tray 'easily compressed': sponge, pillow, stone
2. Tray 'seen through clearly': window glass, cellophane, butter paper
3. Tray 'disappears when stirred in water': sugar, salt, sand
4. Tray 'lustrous': copper wire, aluminium foil, jute rope
Column II
a. Seen through, but not clearly
b. Hard to compress
c. Non-lustrous
d. Stays visible after stirring in water

A primary school in Pune needs drinking cups for 30 Class 1 children for a water break on each of 200 school days, with Rs 1,000 to spend for the year. A shop gives this table.
Material | Holds water? | If a child drops it | Reusable? | Price each
Cloth pouch | No | does not break | Yes | Rs 15
Paper cup | Yes | does not break | No (one use) | Rs 2
Glass tumbler | Yes | breaks | Yes | Rs 40
Steel tumbler | Yes | does not break | Yes | Rs 60
Plastic tumbler | Yes | does not break | Yes | Rs 30
(a) Which two materials does the table rule out by the purpose and by who will use the cups, before any cost is worked out? Give the property for each.
(b) Work backwards: what is the highest whole-rupee price per cup at which 30 reusable cups still fit the budget, and which of the remaining reusable cups pass?
(c) The headteacher says paper cups are cheapest at Rs 2. Show what they would cost for the year.
(d) Which material should the school buy? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Cloth: it cannot hold water, and a cup must. Glass: it breaks when dropped, and small children drop things. (b) Rs 1,000 / 30 = Rs 33.33, so at most Rs 33 per cup; of steel (Rs 60) and plastic (Rs 30), only plastic passes. (c) 30 x 200 x Rs 2 = Rs 12,000 for the year, far over the budget, though each cup is cheap. (d) Plastic tumblers: they hold water, do not break when dropped, can be reused every day, and 30 cost 30 x Rs 30 = Rs 900, within Rs 1,000.
s: Part (a): cloth (cannot hold water) and glass (breaks when dropped)
Part (b): Rs 33 per cup at most; only plastic passes
Part (c): Rs 12,000 for the year
Part (d): plastic, Rs 900, the only cup meeting every need within the budget

questions.q: Four children suggest materials for tumblers to carry drinking water on a school picnic, and each also says why one material must be rejected. Which rejection is NOT a mistake?
questions.a: Reject cotton cloth, since a cloth tumbler cannot hold water
o: Reject cotton cloth, since a cloth tumbler cannot hold water
Reject steel, since steel slowly dissolves in drinking water
Reject plastic, since a plastic tumbler is not made of metal
Reject glass, since a see-through tumbler lets water leak out

questions.q: A craft-fair stall sells cooking pots made of thick paper as an 'eco-friendly' choice. Would you buy one for boiling dal? Give two reasons based on the properties of materials.
questions.a: No. Any two property-based reasons, e.g. a pot for boiling dal must hold water, but paper-like material soaks it up instead of holding it; wet paper turns soft and loses its shape; paper would char or burn over the flame. The material does not suit the purpose of a cooking pot.
s: First property-based reason (e.g. paper soaks up water and cannot hold it)
A second, different property-based reason (e.g. it goes soft and loses shape when wet, or it would burn over the flame)

questions.q:
Ten objects lie on a table: steel spoon, glass tumbler, wooden ruler, plastic water bottle, copper wire, rubber eraser, glass marble, plastic comb, iron nail, wooden spoon.
(a) Classify them into metals and non-metals and give the number in each group.
(b) Classify them into 'used for eating or drinking' and 'not used for eating or drinking' and give the numbers.
(c) Which object is in the metal group and in the eating-or-drinking group?
(d) Why did the groups and their sizes change from (a) to (b)?
(e) Which of the two groupings would a kitchen use to arrange its shelves? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Metals: steel spoon, copper wire, iron nail (3); non-metals: the other 7. (b) Eating or drinking: steel spoon, glass tumbler, plastic water bottle, wooden spoon (4); not: 6. (c) The steel spoon. (d) A different common property was chosen, and the same objects can be classified in more than one valid way. (e) By use, because a kitchen keeps similar utensils together so they are easy to find.
s: Part (a): 3 metals and 7 non-metals listed
Part (b): 4 and 6 listed
Part (c): steel spoon
Part (d): change of common property explains the change
Part (e): grouping by use, with the reason

questions.q: A family in Shimla wants a chair that they will carry up to the terrace and back every day. Chairs are available in iron, plastic, bamboo and stone. Name the two materials you would choose and the two you would avoid, and give the property that decided your choice.
questions.a: Choose plastic and bamboo, because they are light and easy to carry. Avoid iron and stone, because they are heavy to lift every day. The deciding property is how heavy or light the material is (with enough hardness for sitting).
s: Two light materials chosen: plastic and bamboo
Two heavy materials avoided: iron and stone
Deciding property named: light weight for carrying

questions.q:
Six objects: copper wire, glass jar, cloth bag, iron nail, plastic bottle, paper sheet.
(a) Sort them using two properties at once, metal or not metal, and can hold water or cannot, into four boxes: metal and holds water; metal and cannot; not metal and holds water; not metal and cannot.
(b) Which box is empty? Name an everyday object that would fill it.
questions.a: (a) Metal and holds water: none. Metal and cannot hold water: copper wire, iron nail. Not metal and holds water: glass jar, plastic bottle. Not metal and cannot hold water: cloth bag, paper sheet. (b) The 'metal and holds water' box; e.g. a steel tumbler or a copper pot.
s: Part (a): all six placed correctly in the four boxes
Part (b): metal-and-holds-water box empty, with a fitting object such as a steel tumbler

questions.q:
Statement 1: Every metal always shows lustre on its surface, however old the object is.
Statement 2: Because rubber is non-lustrous, no rubber object can ever be made to look shiny.
Statement 3: The freshly cut surface of a metal usually shows more lustre than an old surface of the same metal.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only
o: Statement 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q: A roadside seller says, 'This bangle is pure gold; look how brightly it shines.' Give two reasons why its shine alone does not prove that it is gold.
questions.a: First, not all materials that shine are metals: a non-metal can be made shiny by polishing or a thin coating. Second, even if it is a metal, many metals such as iron, copper, zinc and aluminium are also lustrous, so shine does not tell which metal it is.
s: Reason 1: a shine can come from a coating or polishing on a non-metal
Reason 2: many other metals are lustrous too, so shine does not identify gold

questions.q: Shreya does the sorting challenge in a storeroom with no window and the light switched off. The aluminium foil, the brass key and the cardboard all look equally dull to her. What should she conclude?
questions.a: Nothing yet; she should look again where light falls on them
o: Nothing yet; she should look again where light falls on them
The foil and the key have lost their lustre to air and moisture
All three are non-lustrous, since none of the three of them shines
The foil and the key were only coated, and the coating wore off

questions.q:
A school drama group in Bhubaneswar needs 30 crowns that shine like gold on stage, and has Rs 1,500. Brass crowns, cut from brass sheet (a metal), cost Rs 90 each. Cardboard crowns covered with a thin shiny golden plastic film cost Rs 25 each. Between the yearly shows the crowns lie for 11 months in a damp storeroom.
(a) Which crowns are lustrous because of the material itself, and which only look lustrous? Give a reason for each.
(b) Work backwards from the budget: if every crown not made of brass is a film crown, what is the largest number of brass crowns the group can buy, and what do the 30 crowns then cost?
(c) A teacher says, 'By next year the brass crowns will look dull, so they will have stopped being metal and their shine is gone for good.' Accept or reject her claim, giving a reason for each part of it.
questions.a: (a) Brass crowns: brass is a metal, and metals are lustrous. Film crowns: cardboard is non-lustrous; the shine comes only from the thin plastic coating. (b) All 30 as film crowns cost 30 x Rs 25 = Rs 750, leaving Rs 750; each brass crown in place of a film crown adds Rs 90 - Rs 25 = Rs 65, and Rs 750 / Rs 65 = 11.5, so 11 brass crowns and 19 film crowns, costing 11 x Rs 90 + 19 x Rs 25 = Rs 990 + Rs 475 = Rs 1,465. (c) Reject. Brass kept in damp air may lose its lustre, because air and moisture dull some metals, but it is still a metal; and its shine is not gone for good, because a freshly exposed surface of the metal still shows lustre.
s: Part (a): brass lustrous as a metal; film crowns shine only from a coating
Part (b): 11 brass and 19 film crowns, Rs 1,465
Part (c): claim rejected: a dulled metal is still a metal, and a fresh surface still shines

questions.q:
In a sorting challenge Shreya notes: copper wire - shiny, reddish-brown; aluminium foil - shiny, silvery; cardboard - dull, brown; brass key - shiny, yellow; chalk - dull, white.
(a) Group the five pieces first by shine, then by colour (brown or not brown).
(b) Which piece is in the shiny group but brown, and which is in the dull group but not brown? What do these two pieces show about grouping by appearance?
questions.a: (a) By shine: shiny - copper wire, aluminium foil, brass key; dull - cardboard, chalk. By colour: brown - copper wire, cardboard; not brown - aluminium foil, brass key, chalk. (b) The copper wire (shiny but brown) and the chalk (dull but not brown). Because of them the two groupings do not match: appearance has more than one feature, a different feature gives different groups, and only shine keeps the metals together.
s: Part (a): both groupings correct
Part (b): copper wire and chalk; a different feature gives different groups, and lustre is the one that groups the metals

questions.q: A tray holds an iron nail, a copper wire, a gold ring, a sheet of paper, a rubber band, a piece of aluminium foil, a jute rope and an old zinc sheet that looks dull grey. If a small piece of each is cut off and the fresh surface is looked at straight away, the number of fresh surfaces expected to be lustrous is ___.
Show that the rule 'shiny means metal, dull means non-metal' cannot sort this group correctly: an old iron gate, a wax-polished wooden floor, new aluminium foil, a jute bag.
questions.a: By the rule: aluminium foil (shiny) is a metal and the jute bag (dull) is a non-metal, which is right. But the old iron gate is dull and would be called a non-metal, though iron is a metal that has lost lustre to air and moisture; and the wax-polished floor shines and would be called a metal, though wood is non-lustrous. Two of the four are sorted wrongly, so the rule cannot work.
s: Rule applied to all four items
Iron gate shown wrongly sorted, with the air-and-moisture reason
Polished floor shown wrongly sorted, with the coating reason

questions.q: A copper vessel kept for months in a damp storeroom now looks dull. Arjun wants to use lustre to check whether it is really a metal. What should he do?
questions.a: Scrape a tiny spot and see whether the fresh surface shines
o: Scrape a tiny spot and see whether the fresh surface shines
Polish it with wax and see whether the vessel starts to shine
Compare its colour with that of a new aluminium vessel
Press it with a thumb and see whether it is hard to compress

questions.q:
Ten pieces are collected: paper, cardboard, wood, chalk, copper wire, aluminium foil, a brass key, a steel spoon, a wax-coated paper plate and an old dull iron nail.
(a) Sort them by how they look into 'shiny' and 'not shiny', giving the number in each group.
(b) How many of the ten are metals?
(c) Name the pieces that the rule 'shiny means metal' would sort wrongly.
(d) Give the reason each of them is sorted wrongly.
(e) What should a student conclude about using appearance alone to identify metals?
questions.a: (a) Shiny: copper wire, aluminium foil, brass key, steel spoon, wax-coated plate (5). Not shiny: paper, cardboard, wood, chalk, old iron nail (5). (b) 5: copper, aluminium, brass, steel and iron. (c) The wax-coated paper plate and the old iron nail. (d) The plate shines only because of its wax coating, while paper is non-lustrous; the nail is iron, a metal that has lost its lustre to air and moisture. (e) Lustre usually points to a metal, but appearance alone can mislead; a freshly cut surface is a better check.
s: Part (a): 5 shiny and 5 not shiny, correctly listed
Part (b): 5 metals
Part (c): wax-coated plate and old iron nail
Part (d): coating and air-and-moisture reasons
Part (e): appearance alone can mislead; check a fresh surface

questions.q:
A class scrapes a small spot on each sample and compares the look before and after. Match each sample (Column I) with what the class should see (Column II).
Column I
1. A copper coin left for months in a damp drawer
2. A wax-polished wooden spoon
3. A new steel spoon
4. A rubber eraser
Column II
a. Shiny before scraping and shiny after
b. Dull before scraping but shiny after
c. Dull before scraping and dull after
d. Shiny before scraping but dull after

True or False? A freshly cut surface shows a material's own appearance, so planing a fresh spot on a wax-polished wooden table top will make that spot shine even more than the rest. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A fresh surface does show the material's own appearance, but wood is non-lustrous: the table shone only because of its wax coating. The freshly planed spot will look dull, not shinier. (For a metal, a fresh surface would shine.)
s: Verdict: False
Reason: wood is non-lustrous and the shine came from the wax, so the fresh spot looks dull

questions.q: Kavya sorts objects twice, first by lustre and then by hardness. Which pair lands in DIFFERENT groups when sorted by lustre but in the SAME group when sorted by hardness?
questions.a: A steel spoon and a piece of stone
o: A steel spoon and a piece of stone
A copper wire and aluminium foil
A rubber eraser and a piece of sponge
A sheet of paper and a piece of jute

questions.q: Meher sorts five objects by how they look and writes: Metals - aluminium foil, a wax-coated paper plate, a steel spoon. Non-metals - an old dull copper coin, a jute bag. She claims: 'At most one object is in the wrong group.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Two objects are in the wrong group. The wax-coated paper plate shines only because of its wax coating; paper is non-lustrous and not a metal. The old copper coin looks dull because air and moisture have dulled it, but copper is a metal, and a freshly scratched spot would shine. Foil, spoon and jute are placed correctly.
s: Verdict: no, two objects are misplaced
Wax-coated plate: shine from a coating on a non-metal
Old copper coin: a metal dulled by air and moisture

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An old iron gate looks dull, yet a spot freshly scraped on it shines.
Reason (R): Materials with lustre are usually metals.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) The saying 'All that glitters is not gold' warns about one mistake in sorting materials by appearance. Say what the mistake is and why it happens.
(b) Write a short saying of your own that warns about the opposite mistake, and give one example of an object it fits.
questions.a: (a) The mistake is taking every shiny object to be a metal (or gold). It happens because the surfaces of some materials are made shiny by polishing or by coating them with a thin layer of plastic, wax or another material, and these materials may not be metals. (b) E.g. 'Not all that looks dull is a non-metal.' Example: an old copper vessel or iron gate, a metal that has lost its lustre because of air and moisture. Any fitting saying and example is accepted.
s: Part (a): shiny taken for metal, because polish or a coating can make a non-metal shine
Part (b): a saying about dull metals with a fitting example

questions.q:
A kabadiwala in Kanpur pays Rs 32 per kg for iron, Rs 12 per kg for plastic and Rs 14 per kg for newspaper. A family brings 4 kg of old, dull iron pipes, 2 kg of shiny silver-coloured plastic decorations and 3 kg of newspaper. His new helper sorts only by looks and puts the decorations with the metals and the pipes with the plastic.
(a) Suggest a quick check the kabadiwala can make to show that the dull pipes are a metal.
(b) Why are the shiny decorations not a metal even though they glitter?
(c) How much should the family be paid, and how much less would they get if the helper's sorting were used?
(d) Should the kabadiwala let his helper sort by looks to save time? Decide, using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Scrape or cut a small spot: a fresh iron surface shines, showing the pipes are a metal dulled by air and moisture. (b) Their shine comes from a coating or polish on plastic, a non-metal; not everything that shines is a metal. (c) Correct: 4 x 32 + 2 x 12 + 3 x 14 = Rs 194. Helper: 4 x 12 + 2 x 32 + 3 x 14 = Rs 154, so the family would get Rs 40 less. (d) Sorting by looks is fast but is wrong whenever a metal has turned dull or a non-metal is coated, and here it cost the family Rs 40; he could let the helper sort quickly but check doubtful dull or very shiny items with a scrape test.
s: Part (a): scrape test showing fresh lustre
Part (b): shine from a coating on a non-metal
Part (c): Rs 194 and Rs 40 less
Part (d): justified decision weighing speed against the Rs 40 error

questions.q: A carpenter in Saharanpur wants a wooden toy to look shiny at a fair, and a coppersmith wants an old, dull copper pot to shine again without adding anything to its surface. Which pair of plans works?
questions.a: Toy: coat it with wax; pot: scrape off the dull surface
o: Toy: coat it with wax; pot: scrape off the dull surface
Toy: cut a fresh surface; pot: coat it with a thin wax layer
Toy: cut a fresh surface; pot: scrape off the dull surface
Toy: coat it with wax; pot: leave it in moist air for a week

questions.q:
A box holds five pieces: a piece of jute, an old iron nail, a wax-coated paper plate, a sheet of aluminium foil and a stick of chalk. A mystery piece is picked using two clues.
Clue 1: It does not shine as found.
Clue 2: A freshly scraped spot on it shines.
Say which pieces each clue rules out, name the mystery piece, and explain why it looked dull as found.
questions.a: Clue 1 rules out the aluminium foil and the wax-coated plate, which shine as found. Clue 2 rules out the jute and the chalk, which are non-lustrous and stay dull when scraped. The mystery piece is the old iron nail: iron is a metal that has lost its lustre because of air and moisture, so only its fresh surface shines.
s: Clue 1 rules out the foil and the coated plate
Clue 2 rules out the jute and the chalk
Iron nail named, dulled by air and moisture

questions.q:
Freshly cut, unpolished wood looks quite different from iron, and iron also looks different from copper.
(a) Name one feature of appearance that iron and copper share but freshly cut wood lacks.
(b) Name one feature that tells iron and copper apart, and say why that feature could not be used to put all metals into one group.
questions.a: (a) Lustre: freshly cut iron and copper both have a shiny surface, while wood is non-lustrous. (b) Colour: iron is grey and copper is reddish-brown. Metals differ in colour (aluminium is silvery, gold is yellow), so colour would split the metals into different groups; it is the shared lustre that groups them.
s: Part (a): both lustrous; wood is not
Part (b): colour differs, and metals of different colours would fall into different groups

questions.q: Before a festival, the caretaker of a temple in Madurai finds that its copper lamps look dull. One helper suggests scrubbing away the dull outer surface; another suggests brushing on a thin layer of clear coating. (a) Explain why the lamps became dull. (b) If the dull outer surface is scrubbed away, what kind of surface is exposed, and why would it shine? (c) Explain how a clear coating can make even a non-metal look shiny. (d) After one method a brass lamp and a plastic lamp painted to look like copper would both shine; after the other, only the metal lamp would. Which method is which? (e) The caretaker also wants to check that a newly donated lamp is really a metal. Which method would let him check, and why?
questions.a: (a) Copper is a metal that loses its lustre over time because of the effect of air and moisture on it. (b) Fresh metal, not yet acted on by air and moisture, is exposed; like a freshly cut surface, it shows the metal's lustre. (c) A thin layer of plastic, wax or a similar material makes a surface look shiny, whatever is underneath. (d) The coating makes both lamps shine, because it gives shine to any surface; scrubbing makes only the metal lamp shine, because only a metal has a lustrous fresh surface. (e) Scrubbing a small spot: if the fresh surface shines, the lamp is a metal. A coating would make it shine whatever it is made of, so it proves nothing.
s: Part (a): air and moisture dull the copper
Part (b): fresh metal is exposed and shows lustre
Part (c): a thin coating gives shine to any surface
Part (d): coating shines on both; scrubbing only on the metal
Part (e): scrub a spot, since a coating cannot tell metal from non-metal

questions.q: Ira tests a stick of chalk. She says: 'I cannot squeeze this chalk with my fingers, so a metal key will not be able to scratch it either, and the key test will show that chalk is hard.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Being hard to squeeze with the fingers does not mean a material is hard to scratch; the two tests need not agree. A metal key scratches chalk easily, and a material that is scratched easily is soft. So by the key test chalk is soft compared with the key's metal, and her prediction is wrong.
s: Verdict: no, the claim is wrong
Hard to squeeze does not mean hard to scratch
Chalk is easily scratched by a key, so it is soft compared with it

questions.q: Asha presses four materials with the same force and measures how far her thumb sinks in: sponge 15 mm, a lump of clay 6 mm, a rubber ball 3 mm, a wooden block 0 mm. Her friend says, 'Clay is soft.' Which statement about the clay is correct?
questions.a: Clay is hard compared with sponge but soft compared with rubber
o: Clay is hard compared with sponge but soft compared with rubber
Clay is soft compared with all three, since the thumb sinks into it
Clay is harder than rubber, since it is a solid lump and not a ball
Clay is exactly as soft as sponge, since the thumb sinks into both

questions.q: Three mystery materials are tested. P keeps its shape when pressed and disappears when stirred in water. Q keeps its shape when pressed and stays unchanged in water. R changes shape easily when pressed and stays unchanged in water. Which list could be P, Q and R, in that order?
questions.a: Salt crystal, stone, sponge
o: Salt crystal, stone, sponge
Sand grain, sugar crystal, sponge
Sugar crystal, sponge, stone
Sponge, stone, salt crystal

questions.q:
A class counts the strokes of a steel key needed to leave a clear scratch on six materials: candle 1, chalk 2, wood 4, aluminium 7, iron not scratched after 20 strokes, stone not scratched after 20 strokes.
(a) Rank the materials from softest to hardest as far as the data allows.
(b) Which two materials cannot be ranked against each other with this data, and why?
(c) Which materials are soft compared with wood, and which are hard compared with it?
(d) A student writes 'aluminium is soft'. Explain why this is incomplete.
(e) Suggest one change to the test that could help rank the two materials in (b).
questions.a: (a) Candle, chalk, wood, aluminium, then iron and stone. (b) Iron and stone: neither was scratched in 20 strokes, so the data does not show which is harder. (c) Soft compared with wood: candle and chalk. Hard compared with wood: aluminium, iron and stone. (d) Hardness is relative: aluminium is soft compared with iron and stone but hard compared with candle, chalk and wood, so the comparison must be stated. (e) E.g. try more strokes, or try scratching iron with the stone and the stone with iron to see which one marks the other.
s: Part (a): correct ranking
Part (b): iron and stone, with the reason
Part (c): both groups compared with wood
Part (d): hardness needs a comparison
Part (e): a sensible change to the test

questions.q: True or False? A brick and a stone can both be called hard materials, and yet one of them can still be softer than the other. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Both are hard compared with materials such as sponge or an eraser, but hardness is relative, so when the brick and the stone are compared with each other, one can be scratched or worn more easily and is softer than the other.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: 'hard' is a comparison, so two hard materials can still differ in hardness

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A rubber eraser that a metal key scratches easily can still be called hard when it is compared with a sponge.
Reason (R): A material that sinks in when pressed by hand is soft compared with every other material.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur must re-tile a busy corridor using 200 tiles. Samples are scratched with a steel key and the strokes needed to leave a mark are counted: rubber tile 2, wooden tile 3, cement tile 12, stone tile not marked after 30 strokes. Price per tile: rubber Rs 50, wood Rs 60, cement Rs 35, stone Rs 80. The school's rule: a tile must need at least 10 strokes to be marked.
(a) Which tile is the hardest, and which is softer, rubber or wood?
(b) Which tiles pass the school's rule?
(c) Find the cost of 200 tiles for each tile that passes, and the difference.
(d) A parent says stone must be bought because it is the hardest. Judge this, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Stone is the hardest. Rubber is softer than wood, as it was marked in fewer strokes (2 against 3). (b) Cement (12 strokes) and stone (more than 30). (c) Cement: 200 x Rs 35 = Rs 7,000; stone: 200 x Rs 80 = Rs 16,000; difference Rs 9,000. (d) The parent is not right: hardness only needs to be enough for the purpose, and cement already passes the rule. Stone's extra hardness would cost Rs 9,000 more, so cement is the sensible buy.
s: Part (a): stone hardest; rubber softer than wood
Part (b): cement and stone
Part (c): Rs 7,000, Rs 16,000, difference Rs 9,000
Part (d): cement, since it meets the rule and saves Rs 9,000; hardness judged against the purpose

questions.q:
A shoe company presses three sole materials under the same load. Sponge sinks in by 20 mm, rubber by 4 mm and wood by 0 mm. A good sole must not sink by more than 5 mm, so it does not wear flat, but must give a little (more than 0 mm), so it is comfortable.
(a) Which material meets both conditions?
(b) Use the idea that hardness is relative to explain why each of the other two fails.
questions.a: (a) Rubber (4 mm is more than 0 mm and not more than 5 mm). (b) Sponge is softer than rubber and sinks 20 mm, far more than 5 mm, so it would wear flat; wood is harder than rubber and does not give at all, so it would be uncomfortable. Rubber is hard compared with sponge but soft compared with wood, which is what the sole needs.
s: Part (a): rubber, checked against both limits
Part (b): sponge too soft, wood too hard, rubber in between

questions.q: Strokes of a metal key needed to leave a clear scratch: candle 1, wood 4, aluminium 7, iron not scratched in 20 strokes. A new sample needs 5 strokes. Of the four listed materials, the softest one that is still harder than the new sample is ___.
questions.a: aluminium

questions.q: During a class discussion on hard and soft materials, four students make a statement each. Which statement is NOT correct?
questions.a: Hard compared with one material means hard compared with all
o: Hard compared with one material means hard compared with all
Rubber is harder than a sponge but softer than a piece of iron
A material that a metal key scratches easily is a soft material
A stone is more difficult to compress with the hand than an eraser

questions.q:
(a) A hand-exercise ball is squeezed many times a day to build a strong grip. Should its material be soft or hard compared with a cricket ball? Give a reason.
(b) Why would a cricket ball make a poor hand-exercise ball, and what does this show about choosing a material?
questions.a: (a) Soft: it must be compressed easily when squeezed by the hand. (b) A cricket ball is hard and is hardly compressed by the hand, so squeezing it would not work the grip. A material is chosen for the property its purpose needs, and the same hard material that suits cricket does not suit a squeeze ball.
s: Part (a): soft, as it must compress easily
Part (b): the cricket ball is too hard to compress; material is chosen by the property the purpose needs

questions.q:
Statement 1: Whether a material is called hard or soft is decided by comparing it with another material.
Statement 2: A material that a metal key scratches easily is soft compared with the metal of the key.
Statement 3: A wooden table is hard compared with a woollen sweater.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
A school in Bhopal is choosing a floor mat for its gymnastics room. Each 50 mm thick sample is tested by standing the same sandbag on it and measuring how far it sinks.
Mat | Material | Sinks by
P | foam sponge | 40 mm
Q | rubber | 12 mm
R | cotton-filled | 25 mm
S | coir | 18 mm
The coach's rule: a mat must sink by at least 15 mm, to cushion a landing, and by at most half its thickness, so that ankles do not twist. Among mats that pass, she wants the one that cushions most.
(a) The seller says, 'Mat Q is the hardest, so it is the safest.' Decide first: accept or reject his claim?
(b) Arrange the mats from hardest to softest and say what in the table shows it.
(c) Which mats pass the coach's rule, and which part of the rule does each failing mat break?
(d) Which mat should she buy, and why does this show that neither 'the hardest' nor 'the softest' is the right target?
questions.a: (a) Reject. (b) Q, S, R, P: under the same load, the less a mat sinks, the harder it is. (c) The upper limit is half of 50 mm = 25 mm. R (25 mm) and S (18 mm) pass. Q (12 mm) breaks the lower limit, being too hard to cushion; P (40 mm) breaks the upper limit, being too soft. (d) R: it passes and sinks most (25 mm against 18 mm), so it cushions most. The hardest mat, Q, and the softest, P, both fail; hardness is relative, and the purpose decides how hard is right.
s: Part (a): the claim rejected
Part (b): Q, S, R, P, judged by how far each sinks
Part (c): R and S pass; Q too hard (below 15 mm), P too soft (above 25 mm)
Part (d): Mat R, and both extremes fail the purpose

questions.q:
A thin plastic water bottle dents when squeezed by hand, but a steel tumbler does not. Rita calls the bottle hard; Sam calls it soft.
(a) Explain how each of them can be right.
(b) Arrange the bottle, a woollen sweater and a wooden table from softest to hardest, and say what test you would use.
questions.a: (a) Hardness is relative. Compared with the steel tumbler, the bottle is soft, because it dents under the hand; compared with a woollen sweater, it is hard, because it keeps its shape much better. Each is right only once the comparison is stated. (b) Sweater, bottle, table: press each with the hand and see how easily it is compressed (the sweater most, the table not at all).
s: Part (a): soft compared with the tumbler, hard compared with a softer object such as the sweater
Part (b): sweater, bottle, table, by a pressing test

questions.q: A metal key scratches wax easily and chalk a little less easily, but leaves no mark on a glass marble. A corner of the chalk stick scratches the wax. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: Chalk is hard compared with wax but soft compared with the glass
o: Chalk is hard compared with wax but soft compared with the glass
Chalk is soft, since a key scratches it, so it is softer than wax
Wax is harder than chalk, since the key scratched it most easily
The glass is soft, since the key could not leave any mark on it

questions.q:
Use these clues to arrange sponge, rubber, wood and iron from softest to hardest, giving the clue that places each one.
Clue 1: Rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron.
Clue 2: An eraser can be squeezed by hand, but a wooden block cannot.
Clue 3: A metal key scratches wood easily but hardly marks iron.
questions.a: Sponge, rubber, wood, iron. Clue 1 puts sponge below rubber and iron above it. Clue 2 shows rubber is easily compressed while wood is not, so wood is harder than rubber. Clue 3 shows wood is scratched more easily than iron, so iron is the hardest.
s: Correct order: sponge, rubber, wood, iron
Rubber placed below wood using the pressing clue
Iron placed above wood using the scratching clue

questions.q:
A metal key scratches material P easily. A corner of P can scratch material Q.
(a) Which is harder, P or Q?
(b) Is Q hard or soft compared with the metal of the key? Explain the chain of comparisons.
questions.a: (a) P: it scratches Q, so Q is scratched more easily and is the softer of the two. (b) Soft: Q is softer than P, and P is softer than the key's metal (the key scratches it easily), so Q is also softer than the key's metal.
s: Part (a): P is harder, because it scratches Q
Part (b): Q is soft compared with the key, through Q softer than P softer than the key

questions.q: Ana and Babu compare the hardness of a wooden block and an aluminium block. Babu presses each with his thumb; neither changes shape, so he says they are equally hard. Ana counts the key strokes needed to scratch each: wood 4, aluminium 7. Whose method can rank the two blocks, and why?
questions.a: Ana's, since thumb pressing cannot compress either block
o: Ana's, since thumb pressing cannot compress either block
Babu's, since a block that the thumb cannot press is hard
Babu's, since two hard materials always have equal hardness
Neither, since the hardness of two blocks cannot be compared

questions.q: Neel tries to scratch three materials with one another. The stone scratches the wood, the wood scratches the candle, and the candle scratches neither of the others. He has not yet tried the stone on the candle, but he claims: 'The stone will scratch the candle, and the candle is the softest of the three.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The wood scratches the candle, so the candle is softer than the wood; the stone scratches the wood, so the wood is softer than the stone. So the candle is softer than the stone too, and the stone should scratch it. The candle scratches neither of the others and is softer than both, so it is the softest.
s: Verdict: yes, the claim is correct
Chain: candle softer than wood, wood softer than stone, so the stone scratches the candle
Candle softest, as it is softer than both and scratches neither

questions.q:
You are setting up a toddlers' play corner in an anganwadi. You need (i) a floor mat, (ii) building blocks to stack, and (iii) a storage shelf. Available materials: sponge foam, rubber, wood and iron.
(a) Choose a material for each item.
(b) Justify each choice using hardness or softness.
(c) Explain why the material you chose for the blocks is 'hard' for one purpose but might be 'too hard' for another.
questions.a: (a) Mat: sponge foam (or rubber); blocks: wood (or rubber); shelf: wood (or iron). (b) The mat should be soft so a falling child is cushioned; the blocks must be hard enough to keep their shape when stacked; the shelf must be hard so it does not bend under the weight of toys. (c) E.g. wooden blocks are hard enough to stack, which is needed, but they are hard compared with a toddler's head, so a softer rubber block may be safer if children throw them; hardness is judged against the purpose and the comparison.
s: Mat material chosen with softness reason
Block material chosen with hardness reason
Shelf material chosen with hardness reason
Block material shown as hard for one purpose
Same material judged too hard for another, using relative hardness

questions.q: A family building a new house must choose a material for (i) the main door, (ii) the living-room window, (iii) the bathroom window, (iv) a kitchen jar for sugar and (v) the wall between two bedrooms. The choices are wood, clear glass, frosted glass and brick. Assign one material to each and justify every choice by how much can be seen through it.
questions.a: (i) Main door: wood, opaque, so nobody outside can see in. (ii) Living-room window: clear glass, transparent, so the family can see outside clearly. (iii) Bathroom window: frosted glass, translucent, so light comes in but anyone inside cannot be seen clearly. (iv) Sugar jar: clear glass, transparent, so the amount of sugar left can be seen. (v) Bedroom wall: brick or wood, either of which is opaque, so each room is hidden from the other.
s: Main door: opaque material with reason
Living-room window: transparent material with reason
Bathroom window: translucent material with reason
Sugar jar: transparent material with reason
Bedroom wall: opaque material with reason

questions.q:
Match each need (Column I) with the material that suits it best (Column II).
Column I
1. A soft sheet that folds round a sandwich and shows its filling clearly
2. A bathroom window that lets in light but blurs the view of anyone inside
3. A rigid shop-front panel through which the goods inside must be seen clearly
4. The door of a storeroom whose contents must stay hidden
Column II
a. Clear glass
b. Wooden board
c. Cellophane sheet
d. Frosted glass

Nina stirs spoons of milk, a few at a time, into a glass of clean water and tries to read a printed page through it each time. 0 spoons: words clear. 1 spoon: words clear. 3 spoons: words blurred. 6 spoons: words blurred. 10 spoons: words not seen. Between which amounts did the liquid change from translucent to opaque?
questions.a: Between 6 and 10 spoons
o: Between 6 and 10 spoons
Between 1 and 3 spoons
Between 0 and 1 spoon
Between 3 and 6 spoons

questions.q:
Ria says: 'A translucent sheet is half transparent and half opaque, so through it you see half of an object clearly and the other half not at all.'
(a) What is wrong with her description?
(b) Describe correctly what you would see of a friend standing behind a butter-paper screen.
questions.a: (a) Translucent does not mean part clear and part hidden. Through a translucent material the whole object can be seen, but not clearly. (b) The friend's whole shape is seen, but blurred: the outline shows, while details such as the face cannot be made out clearly.
s: Part (a): translucent means the whole object seen, but not clearly
Part (b): the whole friend seen as a blurred shape

questions.q: Lata says: 'Air, water and window glass are all transparent, so every liquid and every gas must be transparent.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Air, water and window glass are indeed transparent: things can be seen clearly through them. But the conclusion does not follow: a material is transparent because of how clearly we can see through it, not because it is a liquid or a gas. Water with a lot of milk stirred into it is still a liquid, yet printed words cannot be seen through it, so it behaves as opaque.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: air, water and glass are transparent
Wrong part: being a liquid or gas does not decide it; a counter-example such as milky water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Frosted glass is transparent because it is made of glass.
Reason (R): Through window glass, objects can be seen clearly.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A tailor holds three sheets up to a bright window. Through muslin she sees the outline of a tree, but not its leaves clearly; through denim she sees nothing; through cellophane she sees the tree clearly. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Muslin is translucent, denim opaque, cellophane transparent
o: Muslin is translucent, denim opaque, cellophane transparent
Muslin is transparent, as the outline of the tree can be seen
Denim is translucent, as daylight falls on its surface
Cellophane is translucent, as it is a thin wrapping sheet

questions.q: True or False? A clear glass bathroom window covered with fine water droplets after a hot bath behaves as a translucent material, even though it is made of clear glass. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Whether a material behaves as transparent depends on how clearly things can be seen through it, not on what it is called. With the droplets on it, things outside are seen, but only hazily, which is how a translucent material behaves; once it is wiped dry, it is transparent again.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: things are seen only hazily through it, so it behaves as translucent until wiped

questions.q:
A school in Guwahati has classrooms facing a busy road and wants one type of window for all of them. It sets two conditions: fewer than 20% of students distracted by the traffic, and no lights needed in the daytime. A survey of 40 students in each of three rooms gives:
Room's windows | Students distracted | Lights in the daytime
Clear glass | 18 | not needed
Frosted glass | 6 | not needed
Closed wooden shutters | 2 | needed all day
(a) Decide first: which window type meets both conditions?
(b) Show the percentage of students distracted in each room.
(c) Classify the three window materials as transparent, translucent or opaque, and use this to explain both the distraction results and the lights.
questions.a: (a) Frosted glass. (b) Clear glass: 18 / 40 x 100 = 45%; frosted glass: 6 / 40 x 100 = 15%; wooden shutters: 2 / 40 x 100 = 5%. Only frosted glass (15%) and shutters (5%) are under 20%, and of these only frosted glass needs no lights. (c) Clear glass is transparent, so the traffic is seen clearly and distracts most; frosted glass is translucent, so the traffic is seen only hazily, yet daylight comes in; wood is opaque, so nothing outside is seen, but no daylight comes in either and lamps are needed all day.
s: Part (a): frosted glass
Part (b): 45%, 15% and 5%, with shutters failing the lights condition
Part (c): transparent, translucent, opaque, linked to the distraction and the daylight

questions.q: Of these eight, a cellophane wrapper, a thin sheet of aluminium foil, a sheet of butter paper, a cardboard box, clean water in a glass bottle, a frosted glass panel, a wooden spoon and a window pane, the number that are opaque is ___.

(a) Describe a simple test, using a printed page, to sort sheets of material into transparent, translucent and opaque.
(b) A student tests sheet Y over a printed page in a dark corner, sees nothing and calls Y opaque. In daylight the same words show through Y, blurred. What is Y really, and what was wrong with the first test?
questions.a: (a) Hold each sheet over the same printed page, in the same good light, and see whether the print is clear, blurred or not seen at all. (b) Y is translucent: in good light the words are seen, but not clearly. The first test was unfair: in the dark nothing can be seen through any sheet, so every sheet must be tested in the same good light.
s: Part (a): a fair test comparing how clearly print is seen, in the same light
Part (b): Y translucent; the dark-corner test was unfair

questions.q: Raj says: 'Water is transparent, so a bucket of water is see-through whatever the bucket is made of.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Looking down from the top, things at the bottom can be seen clearly, because water is transparent. But looking from the side, the light passes through the bucket's wall as well: through a steel bucket nothing can be seen, because metals are opaque, while through a clear plastic bucket things could be seen. What we can see depends on every material between the eye and the object, so the bucket's material does matter.
s: Verdict: no, the claim is wrong
From above, the transparent water lets the bottom be seen
From the side, an opaque steel wall blocks the view, so the bucket's material matters

questions.q: Ritu holds a sheet of kitchen aluminium foil, which is thinner than butter paper, and then a sheet of butter paper up to a lit bulb. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Foil is opaque though thinner; butter paper is translucent
o: Foil is opaque though thinner; butter paper is translucent
Foil is translucent, since it is thinner than butter paper
Both are opaque, as neither shows the bulb clearly at all
Butter paper is transparent, since some light passes through

questions.q:
Kabir places sheets of butter paper, one on top of another, over a printed page and records what he sees.
1 sheet: letters blurred, but the shape of each word can be made out.
6 sheets: nothing of the print can be seen.
He then holds each stack in front of a lit bulb.
1 sheet: a soft glow comes through, but the outline of the bulb cannot be made out.
6 sheets: almost no light comes through.
(a) How does the stack behave (transparent, translucent or opaque) with 1 sheet?
(b) How does it behave with 6 sheets?
(c) What changed between 1 and 6 sheets, though the material stayed the same?
(d) Is it fair to say 'butter paper is opaque' from the 6-sheet result? Give a reason.
(e) Kabir wants a lampshade that hides the shape of the bulb but still lets light through. Should he use 1 sheet or 6 sheets? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Translucent: the print can be seen, but not clearly. (b) Opaque: the print cannot be seen at all. (c) Only the number of sheets (the thickness) changed; more layers let less of the print be seen. (d) Either answer with a reason: e.g. not fair, because a single sheet, the way butter paper is normally used, is translucent; or fair only for a thick pile, since six sheets together hide the print completely. (e) 1 sheet: his bulb test shows it lets light through while hiding the bulb's outline; 6 sheets let almost no light through, so the lamp would hardly light the room.
s: Part (a): translucent with 1 sheet
Part (b): opaque with 6 sheets
Part (c): thickness changed, not the material
Part (d): a reasoned judgement that separates one sheet from the thick pile
Part (e): 1 sheet, translucent, letting light through but hiding the bulb's shape

questions.q:
Statement 1: Air is transparent, which is why we can see a friend standing across the room.
Statement 2: A frosted glass door is opaque, because a person standing behind it cannot be seen clearly.
Statement 3: Metals, such as a steel plate, are opaque.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Ravi says: 'Frosted glass and butter paper are both translucent, so either can be used for a bathroom window.'
(a) Is he right that both have the see-through property the window needs? Explain.
(b) Give a reason, from another property of materials, why butter paper would still be a poor choice.
questions.a: (a) Yes: both are translucent, so light comes in and shapes show, but a person inside cannot be seen clearly. (b) Butter paper is soft and tears or gets scratched easily (and soaks up water in a wet bathroom), while frosted glass is hard; a window needs to last.
s: Part (a): yes, both translucent, so a person inside is not seen clearly
Part (b): another property, e.g. butter paper is soft and tears easily, unlike hard glass

questions.q:
A sweet shop in Lucknow is choosing 12 display containers: clear plastic jars at Rs 120 each, frosted plastic jars at Rs 100 each or steel tins at Rs 150 each. In a one-week trial with 300 customers for each kind of container, the number who had to ask 'What is inside?' was: steel tins 45, frosted jars 18, clear jars 0. The owner wants no customer to need to ask, and has Rs 1,500 to spend.
(a) Classify the three containers as transparent, translucent or opaque.
(b) What percentage of customers asked, for each kind of container?
(c) Explain the three trial results using how much can be seen through each material.
(d) Which containers should the owner buy? Justify using (b) and the costs.
questions.a: (a) Clear jar: transparent; frosted jar: translucent; steel tin: opaque. (b) Steel: 45 / 300 x 100 = 15%; frosted: 18 / 300 x 100 = 6%; clear: 0%. (c) Nothing inside a steel tin can be seen, so most askers came there; through frosted plastic the sweets are seen only hazily, so some still asked; through clear plastic they are seen clearly, so nobody asked. (d) Clear jars: only they gave 0% asking, and 12 x Rs 120 = Rs 1,440 is within Rs 1,500. Frosted jars (Rs 1,200) are cheaper but 6% still asked; steel tins (Rs 1,800) are over budget and hide the sweets.
s: Part (a): transparent, translucent, opaque correctly matched
Part (b): 15%, 6% and 0%
Part (c): results explained by clear, hazy and no view
Part (d): clear jars, Rs 1,440 within Rs 1,500 and the only 0% result

questions.q: For which of these would a translucent material be a poor choice?
questions.a: The front windscreen of a school bus
o: The front windscreen of a school bus
A bathroom window letting light in
A lampshade hiding the bulb's shape
A shower cubicle door in a sports hall

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four lines) in which three people try to hide from a fourth person: one behind a transparent material, one behind a translucent material and one behind an opaque material. Say what the fourth person sees in each case.
questions.a: E.g. At a school fair, Amit hides behind the clear glass of a display case, Leela behind a frosted glass partition and Raju behind a cardboard stall board, while Kiran searches. Kiran sees Amit clearly (transparent), sees only Leela's blurred shape (translucent) and cannot see Raju at all (opaque).
s: A situation with one hiding place of each kind, materials named
What is seen for the transparent and translucent cases
Nothing seen behind the opaque material

questions.q: A hospital ward needs partitions between beds. The nurse at the desk must be able to see whether a patient is sitting up or lying down, but the patient's face should not be clearly visible to visitors. The choices are clear glass, frosted glass and wooden boards. Which would you choose? Give one reason for rejecting each of the other two.
questions.a: Frosted glass, which is translucent: the nurse sees the patient's shape but not clearly. Clear glass is rejected because it is transparent, so visitors would see the patient clearly. Wooden boards are rejected because wood is opaque, so the nurse could not see the patient at all.
s: Clear glass rejected: transparent, patient seen clearly
Wooden boards rejected: opaque, patient not seen at all; frosted glass chosen as translucent

questions.q: A spoon of salt and a spoon of sand are stirred together into a glass of water, and the glass is left to stand. Some of the clear water from the top is then poured into a cup and tasted. It tastes of ___ (salt or sand).
questions.a: salt

questions.q: Four glass tumblers, each two-thirds full of water, get: tumbler 1 sugar and sand; tumbler 2 salt only; tumbler 3 sawdust and salt; tumbler 4 sugar and salt. All are stirred well and left for a few minutes. In how many tumblers will some added material still be seen?

Before stirring, Meera predicts: sugar will disappear, salt will disappear, sand will not disappear, sawdust will disappear, chalk powder will disappear. She stirs each into its own tumbler of water and waits a few minutes. Sugar and salt disappear; sand and sawdust stay visible; chalk powder turns the water white and cloudy, and some powder settles at the bottom.
(a) Which of her predictions were wrong?
(b) What percentage of her five predictions were correct?
(c) Classify all five materials as soluble or insoluble.
(d) Meera says chalk 'half dissolved' because the water changed colour. Correct her.
(e) Is 'it is a white powder like sugar' a good way to predict whether a material is soluble? Give a reason from her results.
questions.a: (a) Sawdust and chalk powder. (b) 3 out of 5 correct = 60%. (c) Soluble: sugar, salt. Insoluble: sand, sawdust, chalk powder. (d) Chalk did not dissolve: a soluble material disappears completely, but the chalk stayed visible as cloudiness and some settled. A change of colour is not dissolving. (e) No: chalk powder is a white powder like sugar and salt, yet it is insoluble, so looks cannot predict solubility; it has to be tested.
s: Part (a): sawdust and chalk powder
Part (b): 60%
Part (c): two soluble, three insoluble
Part (d): chalk stayed visible, so it did not dissolve
Part (e): no, chalk looks like sugar but is insoluble

questions.q:
Ghulan's mother stirs a spoonful of sugar and a pinch of salt into a glass of water with lemon juice to make shikanji. By mistake, two lemon seeds also fall in.
(a) Nothing of the sugar or the salt can be seen, yet the drink tastes sweet and a little salty. What does the taste tell Ghulan about the sugar and the salt?
(b) After stirring, how will the seeds behave differently from the sugar, and which word describes each?
questions.a: (a) The sugar and the salt are still in the water: they have dissolved, not been destroyed. Being soluble, they disappear from view but stay mixed through the drink. (b) The seeds stay visible however long the drink is stirred, while the sugar disappears: the seeds are insoluble in water and the sugar is soluble.
s: Part (a): dissolved and still present, as the taste shows
Part (b): seeds stay visible (insoluble); sugar disappears (soluble)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After a spoon of honey is stirred into a glass of water and left to stand, no separate layer of honey can be seen, and every sip tastes sweet.
Reason (R): Honey is a liquid that mixes completely with water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Sonu writes two results in his notebook. Result 1: 'I stirred a spoonful of salt into a glass of water. It disappeared, and the water tasted of nothing at all.' Result 2: 'I stirred a spoonful of ordinary sand into water for 30 minutes, and it disappeared completely, leaving nothing at the bottom.' Show that neither result can be right.
questions.a: Result 1: salt is soluble, so it disappears, but it is still mixed in the water; the water must taste salty, so 'tasted of nothing' cannot be right. Result 2: sand is insoluble; an insoluble material does not disappear even after stirring for a long time, so sand grains must still be seen in the water or at the bottom. In each case either the material was not what he says or the observation is wrong.
s: Result 1: dissolved salt is still present, so the water must taste salty
Result 2: sand is insoluble and stays visible however long it is stirred
Conclusion: both reports contradict how the materials behave, so neither can be right

questions.q: A pet-shop owner switches off the pump of a crowded fish tank for a day, and the fish keep coming up to the surface. When the pump is switched on again, pushing bubbles of air through the water so that more of the air mixes with it, they stop. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
questions.a: Oxygen from the air dissolves in water, and water animals need it
o: Oxygen from the air dissolves in water, and water animals need it
Oxygen forms a separate layer on top that the fish swim up to reach
The bubbles make the water opaque so that the fish can hide in it
The air makes the dirt in the tank dissolve, so the fish can see

questions.q:
A fisheries officer in Kerala tests three village ponds with a meter that reads how much of a certain gas is dissolved in the water. Fish stay healthy only if the reading is at least 4 units. In Pond C the fish keep coming up to the surface, so a fountain is fitted that splashes its water through the air for 2 hours, and the ponds are tested again.
Pond | Morning reading | After 2 hours of fountain
A | 8 | 8 (no fountain)
B | 5 | 5 (no fountain)
C | 2 | 5
(a) Which gas is the meter most likely measuring, and why does it matter to the fish?
(b) Which ponds were safe in the morning, and by how many units was Pond C short of the safe level?
(c) The officer claims, 'The fountain made Pond C safe, because splashing the water through the air lets more of this gas dissolve.' Does the table support both parts of his claim? Use (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Oxygen: it dissolves in water, and animals living in water need it to survive. (b) Ponds A and B (8 and 5 units, both at least 4); Pond C was short by 4 - 2 = 2 units. (c) Yes. Pond C rose from 2 to 5 units, 3 units more, and 5 is at least 4, so it is now safe; Ponds A and B, without a fountain, did not change, which points to the fountain as the cause. This fits the idea that oxygen from the air dissolves in water when the two are mixed.
s: Part (a): oxygen, needed by water animals
Part (b): Ponds A and B; Pond C short by 2 units
Part (c): claim supported: C rose by 3 to 5 units (safe), A and B unchanged, fitting oxygen dissolving from the air

questions.q:
Arun has four white powders: glucose, salt, chalk powder and wheat flour. He stirs one spoon of each into its own tumbler of water and waits a few minutes.
(a) In which tumblers will the water look clear, with nothing left to see?
(b) Name a pair of powders that this test cannot tell apart, and explain why.
questions.a: (a) Glucose and salt: both dissolve and disappear. (b) Glucose and salt (or chalk powder and wheat flour): both powders of the pair behave the same way in water, so a test of solubility puts them in one group but does not tell which is which.
s: Part (a): glucose and salt
Part (b): a correct pair, because both behave the same way in water and one property cannot separate them

questions.q: Riya shakes mustard oil with water and at once writes 'mixes completely'. Ten minutes later, with the bottle left undisturbed, she sees two layers. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Her entry was too early; the layer shows that oil does not mix
o: Her entry was too early; the layer shows that oil does not mix
The oil mixed at first and then stopped being soluble later on
Both entries are right, as oil dissolves only while it is shaken
The two layers show that the oil has dissolved in the top half

questions.q: Kriti says: 'Sugar and salt are soluble in water, and so are all liquids and all gases.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Sugar and salt are indeed soluble: they disappear on stirring. But not all liquids mix with water; some form a separate layer when left undisturbed. And only some gases dissolve in water; oxygen does, but others do not.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: sugar and salt are soluble
Wrong part: some liquids form a layer and only some gases, like oxygen, dissolve

questions.q: True or False? Water can dissolve a large number of materials, so water left standing long enough in a tumbler with chalk powder will dissolve all of it. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Water dissolves a large number of materials, but not all of them. Chalk powder is insoluble in water: it does not disappear even after long stirring or standing, and it stays visible or settles at the bottom.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: many materials is not all; chalk powder is insoluble and stays visible

questions.q:
Statement 1: Some gases, such as oxygen, dissolve in water.
Statement 2: A material is called soluble if it sinks to the bottom and stays there after stirring.
Statement 3: All liquids mix completely with water, because water is itself a liquid.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A class records what happens to five materials in water.
Glucose: disappears on stirring - soluble
Wheat flour: disappears completely on stirring - soluble
Vinegar: forms a separate layer - does not mix
Mustard oil: forms a separate layer when left undisturbed - does not mix
Honey (stirred well): no layer left - mixes completely
(a) Two entries are wrong. Name them and correct each.
(b) Using the corrected table, how many of the five materials dissolve or mix completely in water?
(c) A student says honey 'cannot really mix with water, because it is sticky like oil'. Use the corrected table to correct him.
(d) A student concludes, 'Liquids mix with water and powders do not.' Use the corrected table to show that this is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Wheat flour: it does not dissolve; it stays visible and the water turns cloudy. Vinegar: it mixes completely with water and leaves no separate layer. (b) 3: glucose, vinegar and honey. (c) Honey, stirred well, leaves no layer: it mixes completely with water, while mustard oil forms a separate layer. Being sticky does not decide whether a liquid mixes with water; only the test does. (d) Glucose is a powder and it dissolves, while mustard oil is a liquid and it does not mix; whether a material is a liquid or a powder does not decide it.
s: Part (a): wheat flour corrected to 'does not dissolve'
Part (a): vinegar corrected to 'mixes completely'
Part (b): 3 materials
Part (c): honey mixes completely, unlike oil; stickiness does not decide it
Part (d): glucose (powder, dissolves) and oil (liquid, does not mix) disprove it

questions.q: Four students each give an observation as proof that a powder is soluble in water. Which observation is NOT evidence that it is soluble?
questions.a: It settles at the bottom even after stirring for a long time
o: It settles at the bottom even after stirring for a long time
It can no longer be seen anywhere after it is stirred well
The water tastes of it, yet no grains are seen after stirring
Its grains completely disappear within a few minutes of stirring

questions.q:
(a) Plan a fair test to find out whether honey mixes completely with water: say what you would use, what you would do, and what you would look for.
(b) Why would the same plan give a wrong result for mustard oil if you looked only straight after shaking?
questions.a: (a) Take a transparent glass tumbler of water, stir in a spoon of honey well, leave it undisturbed for some time, and look for a separate layer or honey at the bottom; if none can be seen, honey mixes completely. (b) Just after shaking, mustard oil can look mixed; it forms a separate layer only when left undisturbed for some time, so an early look would wrongly record that it mixes.
s: Part (a): a transparent container, stirring, waiting undisturbed, then looking for a layer
Part (b): oil looks mixed at first; the layer forms only on standing

questions.q: Write two short kitchen situations, two lines each: one in which a cook needs a material that is soluble in water, and one in which it matters that a material is insoluble in water. Name the material in each and explain why its behaviour in water matters.
questions.a: E.g. (1) Making lemonade for guests, a cook stirs sugar into water; sugar is soluble, so it disappears and sweetens every sip evenly. (2) Washing spinach, a cook swirls the leaves in a bowl of water; the sand on them is insoluble, so it does not dissolve but settles at the bottom, and the clean leaves can be lifted out. Any two fitting situations are accepted.
s: A situation that needs a soluble material, named
A situation that needs an insoluble material, named
Each explained by what the material does in water

questions.q: After stirring sawdust into a tumbler of water and waiting, Arya sees the sawdust floating on top and the water below it clear. She writes 'sawdust dissolved, because it did not sink'. What is wrong with her conclusion?
questions.a: The floating sawdust is still seen, so it has not dissolved
o: The floating sawdust is still seen, so it has not dissolved
Sawdust that floats has dissolved in the clear water below it
Only materials that sink to the bottom can be called insoluble
She should have waited until the sawdust dissolved at the top

questions.q:
In the class activity on mixing materials in water, the steps say to use glass tumblers and to wait a few minutes after stirring before writing the observations.
(a) Why are glass tumblers used rather than steel ones?
(b) Why wait a few minutes after stirring before recording?
questions.a: (a) Glass is transparent, so we can see whether the material is still there in the water or has disappeared; steel is opaque and would hide it. (b) A soluble material needs a little time to disappear completely, and an insoluble one shows itself, staying visible, so an observation taken too soon could be wrong.
s: Part (a): transparent glass lets us see whether the material remains
Part (b): waiting lets soluble materials disappear fully and insoluble ones stay visible

questions.q:
A family in Kutch draws water from a well. It looks perfectly clear but tastes salty. After a storm, the nearby river water is brown with fine sand; a 10 L bucket of it left standing for 6 hours turns clear, with a 1 cm layer of sand at the bottom. A neighbour suggests: 'Leave the well water standing for 6 hours too, and the salt will settle out like the sand.'
(a) The well water passes a 'looks clear' test but fails a taste test. What does each test tell the family about the salt?
(b) Why does the sand in the river water collect as a layer instead of disappearing?
(c) Will the neighbour's plan remove the salt? Judge, using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Looking clear shows only that no salt can be seen; the salty taste shows that salt is still there. Salt is soluble: it has dissolved and disappeared from view, but it is still mixed in the water. (b) Sand is insoluble in water: it does not disappear, however long it is stirred, so it stays visible and settles at the bottom when the water is left standing. (c) No. Standing lets only an insoluble material such as sand settle out. The salt has dissolved, so it stays mixed in the water, and after 6 hours the water will taste just as salty.
s: Part (a): clear look shows nothing visible; taste shows dissolved salt still present
Part (b): sand is insoluble, so it stays visible and settles
Part (c): no, dissolved salt does not settle out, only insoluble sand does

questions.q: Four students apply the definition of matter to four things. Whose reasoning is correct?
questions.a: Air in a football is matter: it takes up space and has mass
o: Air in a football is matter: it takes up space and has mass
Oxygen dissolved in water is not matter, as it cannot be seen
Honey is not matter, since it has no fixed shape of its own
A paper cup is matter only while it has some water inside it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A paper cup of water placed on a balance gives a greater reading than the same cup when empty.
Reason (R): Water occupies space.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
